Trying to Conceive

Sperm morphology: understanding the result and fertility options

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sperm morphology describes sperm shape under a microscope. A low percentage of normal forms can be worrying, but one result cannot tell you whether pregnancy is possible. Shape needs interpretation alongside sperm number, movement, repeat samples and the reproductive health of both partners. It does not automatically mean you need IVF or ICSI.

What the laboratory measures

A laboratory assesses features of the sperm head, midpiece and tail using defined criteria. A sperm may fall outside those criteria because of its size, shape or another visible feature. Morphology is reported as the percentage classified as normal forms; it is different from sperm concentration and motility, which describe number and movement.

Strict assessment can classify most sperm as outside the normal-form criteria even in fertile people. The report is not a count of genetically healthy sperm and does not directly measure the chance of pregnancy or a child’s health. A microscope photograph or a home-test claim cannot replace a properly performed semen analysis.

What does 4% mean?

The WHO sixth-edition framework and NICE’s 2026 guidance use 4% normal forms as a lower reference value for the specified laboratory methods. This is not a pass–fail boundary between fertility and infertility. It also does not mean a 4% chance of pregnancy. The method and the laboratory’s reference information matter.

Older bands such as 14%, 10% and 5% should not be used as a universal modern fertility grading system. A higher result cannot guarantee conception, and a lower result does not rule out natural pregnancy. Rare, specific patterns affecting nearly all sperm, such as complete round-headed sperm abnormalities, can have greater significance and need specialist assessment.

Why a repeat sample may be needed

Semen results vary between ejaculates. Follow the laboratory’s instructions about abstinence, collection, transport and reporting a missed part of the sample. Mention recent illness, medicines and collection problems. If a result is abnormal, a clinician usually arranges confirmation rather than deciding treatment from one number.

Timing depends on the findings and local guidance. AUA/ASRM advises considering at least two analyses, ideally at least a month apart; NICE recommends confirmation ideally after about three months, but sooner for no sperm or a very low count. Ask when your repeat and referral should happen; a severe finding is not a reason to wait automatically.

Can abnormal shape prevent pregnancy?

Some sperm-shape abnormalities may interfere with movement or fertilisation, but morphology alone usually predicts fertility poorly. Total sperm number, movement, other semen findings, duration of trying and the egg-producing partner’s age and reproductive health also affect the options. Assessment should consider both partners together when relevant.

Do not assume that a small head means IVF is mandatory or that every abnormal-looking sperm is incapable of fertilisation. A specialist can distinguish an isolated low percentage from a particular severe pattern or several abnormal semen measures. Neither a reassuring morphology score nor a single treatment offers a pregnancy guarantee.

IVF and ICSI are different

In conventional IVF, eggs and prepared sperm are placed together for fertilisation in the laboratory. ICSI is a technique used within IVF: an embryologist injects one sperm into an egg. It may be considered for significant male-factor infertility, some surgically retrieved samples or previous fertilisation failure, depending on the whole assessment.

An isolated low morphology percentage does not automatically require ICSI. ASRM’s 2026 review does not support routine ICSI for people without a male-factor indication, and discusses evidence that low morphology alone need not predict benefit. ICSI can damage an egg, adds procedures and cost, and does not guarantee fertilisation, a healthy embryo or a live birth. Discuss why it is recommended for your situation.

Is it too late to freeze sperm?

A low morphology result does not by itself make sperm freezing impossible or too late. Clinics may consider freezing when sperm count is low, quality is deteriorating, future treatment may affect fertility, or producing a sample later could be difficult. Age, the available sample and the reason for preservation need individual discussion.

Not all sperm survive freezing and thawing. The laboratory can advise on storage, sample suitability and possible later IUI, IVF or ICSI; freezing cannot guarantee a future pregnancy. Before treatment that could damage sperm production, ask promptly about preservation rather than waiting for the morphology to improve.

Lifestyle, heat and supplements

Stopping smoking, avoiding recreational drugs and anabolic steroids, limiting alcohol, eating varied meals and taking appropriate exercise support health. Seek individual support with weight concerns without blame. Reducing excessive heat and reviewing workplace chemical or radiation exposure may be sensible, but no lifestyle change guarantees a better morphology score or pregnancy.

Tight underwear is not a treatment. Heat is associated with reduced semen quality, but it is uncertain whether loose underwear improves fertility. Antioxidants, vitamins and herbal products have uncertain clinical benefit for male infertility; do not buy a promised sperm-shape cure or use high doses without advice. Testosterone taken as a fertility treatment can suppress sperm production. Review prescriptions with the clinician rather than stopping them yourself.

Look for causes, not just a better number

A reproductive clinician may review medical and family history, examine the testes and consider targeted tests. Varicocele, infection, hormonal disorders, genetic conditions, prior surgery or injury, medicines and cancer treatment can be relevant. Hormone tests, genetic tests and imaging are selected for the findings, not automatically ordered for every low morphology result.

Coeliac disease is one possible consideration in unexplained subfertility, not a diagnosis made from sperm shape. NICE advises considering testing in that context. Do not start a gluten-free diet before diagnostic assessment because it can make testing inaccurate. Treatment of an identified condition, including selected varicoceles or hormonal disorders, is individual; it cannot promise normal morphology or pregnancy.

When to seek help

Do not delay assessment of an abnormal semen result or a known fertility problem while trying supplements. In otherwise uncomplicated circumstances, ASRM advises fertility evaluation after 12 months of trying when the egg-producing partner is under 35, after six months at 35 or older, and potentially sooner over 40. Known or suspected male subfertility warrants earlier evaluation. Ask for counselling or emotional support if the result is distressing.

Sperm morphology itself is not an emergency symptom. Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicle pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs immediate emergency assessment; do not drive yourself. A new lump, swelling, change in testicle shape or persistent discomfort needs urgent medical advice, rather than waiting for a fertility appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the full semen report and collection details to the clinician. Ask which method was used, what needs repeating and when a referral is appropriate.

Before agreeing to ICSI or freezing, ask why it suits your complete assessment, what the alternatives are and what it can and cannot achieve.

Review medicines, supplements and exposures with the care team. Get a known fertility problem assessed promptly and seek urgent help for testicle symptoms rather than waiting for another semen test.

How BeMama can help

Sperm shape is one useful laboratory observation, but it cannot label someone fertile or infertile on its own. A proportion below the reference value is not hopeless, and a normal result is not a promise. The goal is an informed fertility plan rather than chasing a single percentage.

When to seek help

Do not self-prescribe testosterone, fertility medicines or high-dose supplements, and do not stop prescriptions without advice. Do not postpone known fertility assessment while trying a remedy. Sudden severe testicle pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest requires emergency assessment now; do not drive yourself. New lumps, swelling or changes need urgent medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Morphology measures sperm shape, not your personal pregnancy probability.
  • The 4% reference value is not a fertility pass–fail test.
  • Repeat testing and the complete assessment matter more than one number.
  • Low morphology does not automatically require ICSI or prevent sperm freezing.
  • Lifestyle support is reasonable, but supplements and treatment cannot guarantee pregnancy.

Frequently asked questions

What is sperm morphology?

It is the microscopic assessment of sperm shape, including the head, midpiece and tail. The percentage describes forms meeting the laboratory criteria, not the percentage guaranteed to fertilise an egg.

Is 4% normal forms a pregnancy success rate?

No. It is a lower laboratory reference value used with specified WHO methods, not your chance of pregnancy. Results above or below it need interpretation alongside the rest of the semen analysis and both partners’ circumstances.

Can pregnancy happen with low morphology?

Yes, it can, but no result guarantees pregnancy. Shape alone is usually a poor predictor; count, movement, repeat samples and reproductive factors in both partners matter. Rare severe patterns need specialist advice.

Does a small sperm head mean I must have IVF?

No. A visible feature or one morphology percentage does not by itself decide treatment. A specialist assesses whether there is a particular severe pattern, other semen abnormalities or another reason for assisted conception.

Does low morphology always need ICSI?

No. ICSI injects one sperm into an egg as part of IVF and is chosen for particular indications. An isolated low percentage does not automatically show a benefit; discuss the reason, alternatives, costs and risks.

Can I freeze sperm after an abnormal result?

Possibly. Low count or deteriorating quality can be reasons to discuss freezing, not automatic exclusions. The clinic assesses the sample and future options; not all sperm survive thawing and storage cannot guarantee pregnancy.

Can vitamins, underwear or a gluten-free diet fix the result?

There is no guaranteed sperm-shape cure. Tight underwear is not treatment, and supplement benefit is uncertain. Coeliac testing may be considered for unexplained subfertility; do not remove gluten before assessment or stop prescribed medicines without advice.

Should I wait three months whatever the result?

No. Repeat timing depends on the finding and local guidance, and severe deficiencies can need earlier confirmation and referral. Sudden severe testicle pain, or testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or testicle pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest needs emergency care now.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
